paragraphs: Reactive Oxygen Species Generation Induced by Coupling Phanerochaete chrysosporium with Intermittent Micro-aeration to Enhance Methane Production
Xuepeng Wanga, Zhenru Wanga, Ying Denga, Haohao Maoa, Qilin Yua, Yaobin Zhanga*
a Dalian University of Technology School of Environmental Science and Technology No.2 Linggong Road, Ganjingzi District. Dalian, Liaoning, 116024, China.
Text S1 The selection of the intensity of intermittent aeration

In the previous study, a high methanogenic performance was observed at an aeration intensity of 7%(VAeration:VReactor)/day, and the abundance of methanogens and antioxidant enzymes-encoding genes in response to oxidative stress significantly increased, enabling methanogenesis to proceed smoothly under intermittent microaeration [1]. In a pure culture experiment, it is observed that the spore suspension of white-rot fungi could grow under aeration intensities of 4%(VAeration:VReactor)/day), 8%(VAeration:VReactor)/day), and 12%(VAeration:VReactor)/day). Increasing the aeration intensities was beneficial to the growth of white-rot fungi (unpublished data). In the present study, in Stage 1 and 2, a conservative aeration intensity (20 mL/day (4%(VAeration:VReactor)/day)) was adopted to enable methanogens to adapt to the micro-aerobic environment. In Stage 3, the aeration intensity was further increased to 40 mL/day (8%(VAeration:VReactor)/day) to promote fungal proliferation. The digestion performance and metagenomic results showed that this aeration intensity did not damage the functioning of the anaerobic microbial community. Although the aeration intensity of 12%(VAeration:VReactor)/day was more favorable for fungal proliferation, the introduction of a large amount of air would reduce the methane proportion in biogas (by more than 5%), which was unfavorable for subsequent purification. Therefore, the aeration intensity was not further increased.
The parameters of electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectrometer

EPR instrument (Bruker, Elexsys II E500-CW-EPR) operating parameters were center field 3500 G; microwave frequency 9.8 GHz; microwave power 2.0 mW; modulation frequency 4.0 G; modulation amplitude 4.0 G; sweep width 200 G; receiver gain 3.54 × 104; time constant 41.0 ms; sweep time 15 s; 15 scans.

The generation of •OH was measured using a fluorescence probe method with 100 µM coumarin [2]. After the reaction, a 0.5 mL sample was collected, and 1 mL methanol was added to terminate the reaction. The sample was centrifuged and filtered through a 0.22 µm membrane. The oxidation product of coumarin by •OH, 7-hydroxycoumarin (7h-COU), was measured using a microplate reader with an excitation wavelength of 350 nm and an emission wavelength of 460 nm. The •OH concentration was then calculated based on 7h-COU/14.5%.

Briefly, approximately 5-10 g of thoroughly homogenized sample was transferred into a pre-weighed, pre-combusted porcelain crucible and dried at 105°C for 6 h to determine TSS. After cooling in a desiccator for 30 min, the crucible was weighed, and the same sample was subsequently combusted at 550°C for 2 h in a muffle furnace to determine VSS. TSS content was calculated as the percentage of residue remaining after drying relative to the initial sample weight, while VSS content was determined as the percentage of weight loss during combustion relative to the initial sample weight. All measurements were performed in triplicate using an analytical balance with a precision of ±0.1 mg, and blank controls were included to ensure measurement accuracy. Before analysis, samples were carefully homogenized to ensure representativeness, and any large particles were crushed or ground to achieve a uniform consistency. This method ensures reliable quantification of solid fractions in sludge and cow manure samples.
The determination of biogas content and volume
The content of biogas was measured with a gas chromatograph (Tianmei, GC-7900, China) with a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) [3] before the volume was measured with a 50 mL glass syringe.

After washing three times with 0.01 M phosphate buffer solution (PBS), 20 μL of the sediment suspensions were coated on a glassy carbon electrode (Φ3 mm, working area: 0.07 mm2) and dried in an infrared oven. Electrochemical tests were performed with an electrochemical workstation (Chenhua, CHI 660). The coated glassy carbon electrode, Ag/AgCl electrode, and Pt electrode were selected as the working electrode, reference electrode, and counter electrode, respectively. The capacitance and resistance of the sediment were assessed with cyclic voltammetry (CV) and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), respectively.

Cyclic voltammetry was performed in the range of -1.0 to 1.0 V (vs Ag/AgCl) at scan rates of 50 mV/s, with 30 mL of 0.01 M PBS as the electrolyte. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy was conducted over a frequency range of 1000 kHz to 0.01 Hz, with a sinusoidal perturbation of 10 mV amplitude to analyze the internal impedances of the sediments. Before the electrochemical tests, the electrolyte in the same concentration was aerated for 40 min with N2 to maintain an anaerobic condition.
Text S5 Determination of Cellulose, Hemicellulose, and Lignin

The contents of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin in the sludge samples were determined using the van Soest method with a semi-automatic fiber analyzer(F1600, Alva, China)[4]. The samples were air-dried or oven-dried at 45°C and passed through a 1 mm sieve. After numbering the filter bags, they were dried at 105°C for 1 hour. The pretreated filter bags were weighed, and a suitable amount of sample was placed in the filter bags and weighed, with empty filter bags serving as blanks. The sealed filter bags were then subjected to a stepwise washing procedure.
Text S6 Measurement of enzyme activity

Laccase (Lac), a copper-containing polyphenol oxidase, decomposes the substrate ABTS to produce ABTS radicals, exhibiting a significantly greater absorbance coefficient at 420 nm compared to the substrate (ml076971, 100T/48S). The rate of increase in these radicals is used to determine laccase activity. In contrast, lignin peroxidase (LiP), a ferrous heme-containing peroxidase, catalyzes the demethylation of asphaltene, resulting in a decrease in absorbance value measured at 651 nm (ml092790, 100T/96S). Likewise, manganese peroxidase (MnP), another ferrous heme-containing enzyme, performs the oxidation of guaiacol to tetra-o-methoxylenol, displaying a distinct absorption peak at 465 nm (ml076964, 100T/96S) [5].

At the end of each stage, 5 mL of sludge samples were collected and frozen at -80℃ before microbial community analysis. DNA was extracted from sludge samples using a rapid DNA extraction kit (Bioteke Corporation, China). For fungal community analysis, the ITS1-ITS2 regions were amplified using primers ITS1F/ITS2R [5]. The purified PCR products were sequenced by the Illumina Hiseq 2000 platform (Shanghai Lingen Biotechnology Co., Ltd.).

At the end of the operation, 5 mL of the sludge samples were collected and frozen at -80℃ before metagenomic analysis. Nine random DNA sequences were synthesized, and their base arrangement was different from that of microbial gene sequences in nature. In the experiment, 9 sequences were set into 4 gradients according to the copy number content, and the multiple of each gradient was 10-fold. These sequences were designed and synthesized by GeneCowin Biotechnologies Inc., Shanghai, China.

The metagenomic absolute quantification sequencing was performed by GeneCowin Biotechnologies Inc., Shanghai, China. Briefly, total genomic DNA was extracted using the FastDNA® SPIN Kit for Soil (MP Biomedicals, Santa Ana, CA) according to the manufacturer's instructions. The integrity of genomic DNA was detected through agarose gel electrophoresis, and the concentration of genomic DNA were detected through the Qubit3.0 Spectrophotometer. The DNA extracts were spiked with internal standard spike-in DNA（Genesky, China） at 0.1% total DNA by mass. The DNA after mixing internal standard spike-in DNA was sheared by Covaris® system (Covaris, USA). DNA libraries were prepared by a ligation dependent method by using DNA library preparation kit (Genesky, China). 500-600 bp range of sequencing library was size-selected and recovered using MagicPure® Size Selection DNA Beads (Transgen，Beijing). DNA libraries were qualified on the Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent, USA), and quantified with Kapa Library Quantification kit (Kapa Biosystems, Wilmington, MA) using the ABI 9700HT Fast Real-Time PCR system (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The libraries were sequenced on NovaSeq 6000 platform (Illumina USA) and generated 10G bps of 2×150bp pair-end reads.

In the sequencing data, internal standard spike-in DNA sequence was first identified and moved out to make the standard curve. Standard curve of each sample was made with the logarithmic value of read-count per unit length as the horizontal coordinate, and the copy number logarithmic value of each gradient sequence in the internal standard spike-in DNA sequence as the vertical coordinate.
